question: Two MFEs are loaded on the same page. Both use the global class `.btn`. Which MFE will 'win' in the CSS cascade?

options.text: The MFE with the higher selector specificity
options.explanation: Both use the same class .btn — specificity is equal. The order is determined not by specificity, but by position in the DOM.

options.text: The MFE loaded last in DOM order
options.explanation: With equal specificity, the CSS cascade applies the rule encountered later in the document. Whoever is loaded last overwrites the styles.

options.text: The MFE registered first in the shell application
options.explanation: Registration order in the config does not determine CSS cascade order. What matters is the physical order of <style>/<link> tags in the DOM.

options.text: The browser randomly picks one of the rules
options.explanation: The CSS cascade is deterministic. With equal specificity, the last encountered rule is applied — this is the W3C standard.

question: CSS Modules generate unique class names. What exactly is added to a class name to ensure uniqueness?

options.text: The name of the component file
options.explanation: The file name is used as a base, but a content hash is appended to it. The file name alone does not guarantee uniqueness when names are identical across different MFEs.

options.text: A hash computed from the file's content or path
options.explanation: The bundler (webpack/vite) computes a hash from the CSS file's content or path. This guarantees uniqueness: .btn → .btn_a3x9k1. Changing the file changes the hash.

options.text: A random number generated at each build
options.explanation: If the hash were random, every build would produce different class names. This would break caching and stability.

options.text: The version of the component's npm package
options.explanation: The npm version does not participate in CSS Modules hash generation. Different components of the same version would have the same hash.

question: What unique property of CSS Custom Properties allows them to be used as a 'bridge' through Shadow DOM?

options.text: CSS Custom Properties have a special status in the Shadow DOM specification
options.explanation: There is no special status. Their behavior is explained by standard CSS mechanisms.

options.text: They are inherited across Shadow DOM boundaries, unlike regular CSS properties
options.explanation: CSS Custom Properties (--var) are inherited throughout the entire DOM tree, including Shadow DOM. This is the only official way to pass style information inside Shadow DOM without direct access to the shadow root.

options.text: Shadow DOM automatically copies CSS Custom Properties from the parent document
options.explanation: Shadow DOM does not 'copy' anything. Custom Properties are inherited through the standard CSS inheritance mechanism.

options.text: CSS Custom Properties only work in light DOM, not in Shadow DOM
options.explanation: This is incorrect. CSS Custom Properties are inherited through Shadow DOM, which makes them the primary mechanism for passing tokens into Web Components.

question: The design system releases version 3.0.0 and renames the token --ds-color-blue → --ds-color-primary. What should be in tokens.css v3.0.0?

options.text: Only --ds-color-primary; the --ds-color-blue token is completely removed
options.explanation: Instant removal will break all MFEs that use --ds-color-blue. This violates the principle of backward compatibility.

options.text: Both tokens: --ds-color-primary with the new value, and --ds-color-blue: var(--ds-color-primary) as a deprecated alias
options.explanation: The correct approach: a new token + a deprecated alias pointing to the new one. Teams get time to migrate. The alias is removed only in the next major version.

options.text: Only --ds-color-blue renamed without an alias, but with a note in the CHANGELOG
options.explanation: The CHANGELOG does not help applications that already use the old token. The code will break before anyone reads the CHANGELOG.

options.text: Both tokens with the same value, without marking deprecated
options.explanation: Adding both without marking deprecated means not signaling to teams that migration is needed. In a few versions, both will have to be removed anyway.

question: A team is choosing between CSS Modules and Shadow DOM for style isolation of a new MFE. Which factor should be decisive in favor of Shadow DOM?

options.text: The MFE must support IE11
options.explanation: Shadow DOM is not supported in IE11. This is an argument against Shadow DOM, not in favor of it.

options.text: The MFE will be used as a reusable Web Component across different applications
options.explanation: Shadow DOM is justified when full DOM structure encapsulation for reuse is needed. If the MFE is just a regular page section, CSS Modules are sufficient and easier to maintain.

options.text: The project uses TypeScript
options.explanation: TypeScript does not influence the choice of CSS isolation strategy. Both approaches are compatible with TypeScript.

options.text: Maximum render speed is required
options.explanation: Shadow DOM has some runtime cost for creating a shadow root and setting up styles. CSS Modules have no runtime cost — everything happens at build time.

question: What is a design token in the context of design systems? Choose the most accurate definition.

options.text: A specific CSS value (e.g., #1976d2) stored in a variable for reuse
options.explanation: This describes a CSS variable, not a design token. A token is an abstraction of a design decision, not just a named value.

options.text: A named variable of a design decision that abstracts semantics from a concrete value
options.explanation: The token --ds-color-primary means 'the primary action color' — the semantics are stable. The value (#1976d2 or #8b5cf6 after a rebrand) can change without changing the token.

options.text: Any CSS Custom Property starting with two dashes (--)
options.explanation: Not every CSS Custom Property is a design token. A component-local variable --local-padding also starts with --, but it is not a design system token.

options.text: A JSON file with component appearance settings
options.explanation: JSON is one of the formats for storing and distributing tokens, but not a definition of the concept itself.

question: CSS Layers (@layer) are declared in order: @layer base, mfe-a, mfe-b. Inside mfe-a there is .btn with background: blue (!important). In mfe-b — .btn with background: red (no !important). What color will .btn be?

options.text: Blue, because mfe-a has !important
options.explanation: !important inside a layer raises priority relative to other rules in the same layer. But between layers, priority is determined by declaration order, and !important works in reverse order for layers.

options.text: Red, because mfe-b is declared later and has higher layer priority
options.explanation: In CSS Layers, a later layer has higher priority for normal rules. !important inside a layer has reversed priority: !important in mfe-a loses to !important in mfe-b, but a normal rule in mfe-b wins.

options.text: Blue, because mfe-a was loaded first
options.explanation: With @layer, load order does not determine the winner. The winner is the layer with the highest priority according to the @layer base, mfe-a, mfe-b declaration.

options.text: The result is unpredictable — it depends on script load order
options.explanation: It is exactly the opposite: the point of @layer is to make the cascade predictable and independent of load order.

question: Which statements about the token distribution strategy via an npm package are correct?

options.text: Updating tokens requires a rebuild and redeploy of all MFE consumers
options.explanation: This is the main drawback of the npm approach. For a token update to take effect, each MFE must update its dependency and be rebuilt.

options.text: Supports TypeScript types and tree-shaking
options.explanation: An npm package can export TypeScript types for tokens and supports tree-shaking — only used tokens will end up in the bundle.

options.text: Allows updating styles in production without deploying MFEs
options.explanation: This describes the CDN or Federated Module approach. An npm package is embedded in the bundle at build time, so an update requires a rebuild.

options.text: Each MFE can use different versions of tokens
options.explanation: Different MFEs can have different versions of @company/design-tokens in their dependencies. This allows gradual migration, but may lead to visual inconsistency.

question: A team is migrating from Shadow DOM to CSS Modules. What problems might they encounter during migration?

options.text: Global page styles can now affect the component
options.explanation: Shadow DOM fully isolates from external styles. CSS Modules only isolate class names, but do not protect against global properties (body font-size, * box-sizing, etc.).

options.text: CSS Custom Properties will stop working inside the component
options.explanation: CSS Custom Properties are inherited in regular DOM just as through Shadow DOM. Switching to CSS Modules does not break CSS variable behavior.

options.text: Component styles need to be rewritten — Shadow DOM CSS is not directly applicable
options.explanation: Styles written for Shadow DOM use :host, ::slotted, and other Shadow DOM-specific selectors. When migrating to CSS Modules, these selectors need to be rewritten.

options.text: A polyfill will be required to support CSS Modules in older browsers
options.explanation: CSS Modules do not require polyfills — they are transformed into regular CSS classes at build time. The browser receives already-transformed CSS.

question: The design system is distributed via Federated Module. On Friday evening, a bug is discovered in a token: --ds-color-error turned out to be orange instead of red. What will happen after fixing and deploying design-system?

options.text: Nothing — MFEs already have their own copies of tokens in their bundles
options.explanation: This describes the npm package approach. With Federated Module, tokens are loaded from the host at runtime, not embedded in the bundle.

options.text: All MFEs will receive the fix on the next page load by the user
options.explanation: Federated Module loads code from a remote URL at runtime. After deploying design-system, the new code with the fixed token will be loaded on the next page open — without rebuilding MFEs.

options.text: The fix will apply instantly to all active sessions
options.explanation: Federated Module is loaded when the page is opened. Users with open tabs will receive the fix only after reloading the page.

options.text: Manual dependency updates in each MFE will be required
options.explanation: This describes the npm approach. Federated Module does not require updating dependencies — the remote URL stays the same, only the content at that URL changes.

question: Why is using !important in design tokens considered a bad practice?

options.text: !important does not work with CSS Custom Properties
options.explanation: !important technically works with CSS Custom Properties. The problem is not a technical limitation.

options.text: !important makes it impossible to override a token at the MFE or component level
options.explanation: One of the primary use cases for tokens is the ability to locally override them (e.g., for a dark theme). !important breaks this mechanism: an MFE won't be able to override a token even in valid cases.

options.text: !important is incompatible with CSS Layers
options.explanation: !important is compatible with CSS Layers, although it has special behavior (reversed priority order between layers). This alone is not a reason to avoid !important in tokens.

options.text: !important increases the CSS file size
options.explanation: Adding !important to each token adds a few bytes, but this is negligible. The real problem is the architectural constraints it creates.

question: Which of the following design token naming approaches is most correct?

options.explanation: These are primitive tokens — they describe a value, not semantics. After a rebrand, --blue-500 might become purple, creating a semantic mismatch.

options.text: --ds-color-primary, --ds-color-error, --ds-spacing-md
options.explanation: Semantic tokens with an explicit namespace (--ds-) and category (color, spacing). They describe purpose, not value. --ds-color-primary means 'the primary action color' regardless of the specific shade.

options.text: --button-background, --header-color, --card-padding
options.explanation: Component tokens — too specific. If a button and header use the same color, you either duplicate the value or reference a semantic token.

options.text: --color1, --color2, --size1, --size2
options.explanation: Unreadable names with no meaning. It is impossible to understand the purpose without documentation. Maintaining such a token system is extremely difficult.
